source_text: Liquet igitur absolutissime nullo Augustinum a praeceptore suo differre, sed disputationibus eius non minus Adae, quam ceterorum naturam pessimam definiri. Denique ut adhuc aliquid cum eodem de his, quae egimus, disseramus, apparet te etiam primi peccati non idem genus, quod aliarum putare culparum. Nam cum dicis flagitia temporum secutorum in naturam transire non posse, verbi gratia, ut de peculatore, de parricida, de incesto orti filii generantum peccatis nascantur obnoxii; nec ullum crimen esse quod seminibus misceatur, praeter illud unum, apertissime ostendis illam inobedientiam non te eiusdem generis arbitrari, cuius etiam ceterae sunt. Vide ergo interrogatio nostra quantae sit brevitatis et lucis. Si peccatum, quod Adam commisit, voluntate susceptum est, et potuit fieri naturale, cur non haec quae fiunt quotidie peccata, quae voluntas criminosa committit, in deformitatem et praeiudicia seminum congeruntur? Quod si ista non minus atrocia, quam plura, ingenerari nequeunt; qua lege, qua conditione, quo privilegio illud solum vindicatur ingenitum? Si unius generis peccata sunt, quae novimus, quae lex arguit, quae aequitas punit, et illud primi hominis, quod voluntate commissum et aequitate punitum est; cur non aut ista ex illo intellegimus, aut illud ex istis? Aut si mutuo sibi testimonio esse non possunt, qua impudentia denegatur illa praevaricatio alterius conditionis fuisse, id est, non de voluntate, sed naturali tabe prolata? Postremo, aude cum assertione traducis definire quodcumque peccatum, non dico illud primum, sed interim vel de his quae nunc fiunt, verbi gratia, sacrilegium, flagitium, vel malum quodpiam facinus; id est, haec peccata quam definitionem habeant, explicato. Dices sine dubio: Voluntas est appetens quod iustitia vetat, et unde liberum est abstinere. Quia si voluntas mala non esset, peccatum esse non posset. Ad hoc quam rationabiliter assurgamus intende. O hebetudinem, o impudentiam non ferendam! Definis non esse peccatum nisi voluntatem liberam, et a iustitia prohibitam, cum mali naturalis opinio praescribat esse peccatum, cum quo nascitur homo, non voluntarium. Non est ergo verum, culpam non esse, nisi quae sponte committitur; quia est crimen, et maximum, quod non sponte, sed nascendo suscipitur. Remitte igitur definitionem peccati, quae Catholicis amica ad vos nec hospitii iure deflectit, atque ea remissa, proba te non esse illorum commilitonem, qui ipsam substantiam invidia pravitatis oppugnant. Et ut quod egimus colligatur: aut nullum docebitur voluntarium, si est aliquod naturale peccatum; aut nullum erit naturale, si omne peccatum voluntarium definitur; conficiturque ex his, ut aut neges nasci posse peccatum, et transeas in Catholicorum fidem; aut si perstiteris non aliquod, sed maximum crimen sine voluntate suscipi per naturam, reddas nomen tuum etiam Manichaeo, cui totum praestas obsequium.
pass_a_gloss: It is therefore most absolutely clear that Augustine differs from his teacher by nothing, but that by his disputations the nature not less of Adam than of the rest is defined worst. Finally that we may still discuss something with the same about those things which we have done, it appears that you think even of the first sin not the same genus which of other faults. For when you say that the outrages of following times cannot pass into nature, for example that sons arisen from an embezzler, from a parricide, from an incestuous one are born liable to the sins of those generating; nor is there any charge which is mixed with seeds, besides that one, you most openly show that you do not judge that disobedience of the same genus, of which even the rest are. See therefore of how great brevity and light our interrogation is. If the sin which Adam committed was taken up by will, and could become natural, why are not these sins which are done daily, which a criminal will commits, heaped into the deformity and prior judgments of seeds? But if these no less atrocious than more cannot be ingenerated; by what law, by what condition, by what privilege is that alone claimed inborn? If sins are of one genus, which we know, which the law accuses, which equity punishes, and that of the first human, which was committed by will and punished by equity; why do we not either understand these from that, or that from these? Or if they cannot be a testimony to each other, by what shamelessness is it denied that that prevarication was of another condition, that is, not from will, but brought forth by a natural wasting? Finally, dare with an assertion of the tradux to define whatever sin, I do not say that first, but meanwhile even from those which are now done, for example sacrilege, outrage, or some evil crime; that is, what definition these sins have, explain. You will say without doubt: It is a will appetizing what justice forbids, and from which it is free to abstain. Because if there were not an evil will, there could not be sin. To this how reasonably we rise, attend. O dullness, o shamelessness not to be borne! You define that there is not sin except a free will, and forbidden by justice, when the opinion of natural evil prescribes that there is sin, with which a human is born, not voluntary. It is therefore not true that there is not fault except which is committed spontaneously; because there is a charge, and a greatest, which is taken up not spontaneously but by being born. Remit therefore the definition of sin, which friendly to the Catholics does not even deflect to you by the right of hospitality, and that having been remitted, prove that you are not a fellow-soldier of those who attack the substance itself by the spite of crookedness. And that what we have done may be gathered: either none will be taught voluntary, if there is some natural sin; or none will be natural, if every sin is defined voluntary; and it is accomplished from these, that you either deny that sin can be born, and pass into the faith of the Catholics; or if you have persisted that not some, but a greatest charge is taken up without will through nature, you may render your name also to Manichaeus, to whom you furnish the whole obedience.

Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil

pass_b_english: It is therefore perfectly clear that Augustine differs in nothing from his teacher. His arguments define Adam’s nature as utterly evil no less than everyone else’s. To discuss further with him what we have treated, it appears that you do not even consider the first sin the same kind as other faults. You say later ages’ crimes cannot pass into nature—for example, that children born from an embezzler, a parent-murderer, or an incestuous person are not born liable for their parents’ sins—and that no crime except that one is mixed into reproductive seed. You therefore show with complete openness that you do not consider that disobedience of the same kind as the rest.

See how brief and clear our question is. If Adam’s sin was adopted voluntarily and could become natural, why are the sins committed every day by a criminal will not piled into the deformity and prejudicial condition of reproductive seed? If these sins, no less atrocious and more numerous, cannot be implanted at birth, by what law, condition, or special privilege is that one alone claimed to be inborn? If the sins we know, which law condemns and fairness punishes, are of the same kind as the first human’s sin, committed voluntarily and punished justly, why do we not understand these from that one, or that one from these? If they cannot testify to one another, how can anyone shamelessly deny that the first transgression was of another condition—produced not by will but by natural corruption?

Finally, while maintaining inherited sin, dare to define any sin. I do not mean the first; for now take one committed today—sacrilege, a shameful act, or some evil crime. Explain the definition of these sins. You will undoubtedly say: It is a will seeking what justice forbids and from which it is free to abstain; if there were no evil will, there could be no sin. Observe how reasonably we rise against this. What dullness, what intolerable shamelessness! You define sin as nothing but a free will forbidden by justice, while the theory of natural evil lays down that there is an involuntary sin with which a human is born. Then it is not true that only what is freely committed is a fault, since there is a crime—and the greatest one—received not voluntarily but by birth.

Give back, then, the definition of sin that is friendly to catholics and does not turn aside to lodge with you even as a guest. Having relinquished it, prove that you are not a fellow soldier of those who attack substance itself with the stigma of wickedness. To gather our conclusions: either no sin will be shown voluntary if any sin is natural, or none will be natural if every sin is defined as voluntary. Consequently, either deny that sin can be born and come over to catholic faith, or, if you persist that not merely some sin but the greatest crime is received through nature without will, give your name too to Mani, whom you obey in everything.

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
